difficultyRationale: Tests whether the candidate knows what least-connections actually tracks, not just that it exists.
prompt: A team switches their load balancer from round-robin to a least-connections algorithm, specifically to fix the uneven overload problem caused by requests of wildly different processing cost. What does least-connections actually do differently that addresses this?
explanation: Least-connections routes each new request to whichever backend currently has the fewest active (in-flight) connections, rather than just the next one in a fixed sequence. Because a slow, expensive request keeps its connection open for longer, the instance handling it naturally accumulates a higher active-connection count and stops receiving new traffic until it finishes — which is exactly the load-aware signal plain round-robin lacks.

options.text: It inspects the CPU and memory utilization reported by each backend's health-check endpoint every few seconds, and routes new requests away from any instance currently above a configured utilization threshold set by the operator.
options.explanation: Least-connections doesn't read CPU/memory metrics at all; it only tracks the count of active connections the load balancer itself currently has open to each backend, independent of any health-check payload.

options.text: It sends each new request to the backend with the fewest currently active connections, so an instance stuck handling a slow request — and therefore holding an open connection longer — naturally receives fewer new requests until it finishes.
options.explanation: Correct. Active-connection count is a live proxy for how busy an instance currently is, regardless of why — a slow request keeps its connection open, which this algorithm sees and routes around, unlike plain round-robin's fixed sequence.

options.text: It pre-classifies every incoming request by its URL path into 'cheap' and 'expensive' buckets using a lookup table, then spreads expensive requests round-robin style across instances separately from the cheap ones.
options.explanation: Least-connections has no concept of a request-cost classification table; it makes its routing decision purely from the current active-connection count per backend, not from inspecting or categorizing the request itself.

options.text: It measures the average response time of each backend's last several requests and routes new traffic toward whichever instance has recently responded fastest, on the assumption that a consistently fast instance currently has spare capacity.
options.explanation: That describes a response-time-based or weighted algorithm, not least-connections — least-connections never looks at historical response times, only the backend's current count of open connections.
